titleStmt.title: Quantifying the Advantage of EDF vs. RMS Schedulability on a Uniprocessor Using a Differential Analysis and a Power-law Total Utilization Distribution

analytic.title: Quantifying the Advantage of EDF vs. RMS Schedulability on a Uniprocessor Using a Differential Analysis and a Power-law Total Utilization Distribution

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Contrary to the optimal scheduling algorithm Earliest Deadline First (EDF), Rate-Monotonic Scheduling (RMS) can lead to non-schedulable task sets for total utilizations below 1 on a uniprocessor. The quantification of this deficiency has been a topic in real-time science for a long time. We show weaknesses of the scheduling algorithm metrics breakdown utilization, utilization upper bound, and numerical optimality degree. Finally, we suggest a new measure of schedulability called Efficiency and calculate its bounds. It turns out that numerical optimality degree might be too optimistic depending on the assumed total utilization distribution. The main results are the application of a power-law total utilization distribution to quantify the RMS-to-EDF Efficiency and a step-by-step derived lower bound of this Efficiency. We apply a differential analysis of schedulability.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Rate-Monotonic Scheduling (RMS) and Earliest Deadline First (EDF) are the two most famous real-time scheduling algorithms [1]. There are several approaches to quantify the difference in uniprocessor1 schedulability between these two algorithms. While the exact schedulability test for implicitdeadline EDF is just a simple utilization bound, namely u ≤ 1, the exact RMS test Time-Demand Analysis (TDA) [3] is quite complicated. A utilization bound for RMS can only be a sufficient test since the crash utilization with first deadline misses highly depends upon period values, and, thus varies between the Liu/Layland (LL) bound (1) [1] in the general 2 case and the u ≤ 1 bound in the most beneficial case of simply periodic (aka harmonic) task sets, see also [4]. This complicated situation raises the question for the average effectiveness of RMS with respect to EDF and its quantification.
A. Related Work
Important approaches for measuring the effectiveness of RMS versus EDF are the following three (in chronological order):

1) Breakdown utilization [3] 2) Utilization upper bound [5] [6] [7] 3) Numerical optimality degree [8] [9] While the deficiencies of the first two approaches have already been discussed to a large extent in [9], this is not the case for the latter suggestion.

The quantification of the RMS-EDF gap by speedup factors [10] for implicit-deadline and constrained-deadline task sets has been achieved by Davis et al. [11]. For the implicit-deadline case, their results are essentially closely coupled to utilization upper bounds since the speedup factors turn out to be the reciprocal values of the bounds.

A formula equivalent to our result (24) for n-task scheduling using RMS was given in [12] by Bini et al. But there, the focus was on the evaluation of the Hyperbolic Bound itself. We embed this special result in the context of bounds for the RMS-to-EDF performance relationship and give explicitly underlying utilization distributions. Additionally, the comparison there is performed on the level of sufficient RMS schedulability tests and the gold reference, the exact test TDA, and not on the level of scheduling algorithms.

Gopalakrishnan [13] tried to determine a sharp threshold of RMS utilization where the probability of being RMschedulable quickly drops from 1 to 0. He could prove its existence but left the concrete value of the threshold as an open problem. Experimentally, he was able to contain the value of the threshold to the interval [0.8, 0.9]. A drawback of the threshold approach is its asymptotic nature making it valid mainly for large task sets. On the other hand, an offline calculation of thresholds for different task set sizes was proposed [13].

In [14], Hermant et al. proposed an efficiency and complexity framework for uniprocessor scheduling algorithms. Their A-to-B efficiency for two scheduling algorithms A and B is defined as the maximum of all possible norm ratios between the schedulability regions of A and B. They showed that an RM schedulability region is in general not convex. Further, the LL bound (1) has been confirmed as an underestimation of their efficiency measure. The lower the dispersion of the periods in the task set, the greater is the degree of underestimation [14]. A consideration of utilization probability distributions is lacking in [14].

A characterization of the RM schedulability region was given in [15]. There, the TDA condition [3] is rewritten in a more expressive form of several inequalities first ORed and then ANDed. By each inequality, a half-hyperspace at one side of a hyperplane is selected. This gives a polytope as schedulability region which becomes quite complex [15]. In [15], there are no attempts to exploit the hypervolume of the polytope for performance measures of RMS.

Besides this concrete quantification question, there were heated debates on the advantages and drawbacks when it comes to a comparison of RMS and EDF. Some misconceptions and common beliefs were corrected and clarified by Buttazzo [16]. By now, the community agrees that RMS and EDF have relative merits to each other. RMS is simple and response-time predictable while EDF can maximize total utilization under real-time guarantee, rendering it an optimal uniprocessor scheduling algorithm. The simplicity of RMS and the direct support of priority levels by common operating systems is still guaranteeing its predominance in uniprocessor scheduling.

div.head: B. Contributions
div.p: In this article, we present a new measure of the RMS-EDF gap coined Efficiency, define it, and calculate its upper and lower bounds. For task sets of sizes 1 and 2, exact Efficiency values are given. The new measure is motivated by our criticism of the measure numerical optimality degree.

Already at this stage, we stress that average case analyses always have to refer to assumed probability distributions of parameters. Important parameters in real-time scheduling are individual task utilizations u i and total utilization u. On the next level, period values P i might have to be considered [17]. Assuming a uniform distribution of them is the simplest approach. It is tempting to base arguments always on uniform distributions, but both for utilizations and periods, this might not be appropriate.

Our approach is based on the intuition that task set samples of higher total utilizations are more valuable, a line of argument also taken when the performance metric weighted schedulability was introduced in [18].

div.head: C. Structure
div.p: The rest of this article is structured as follows. Section II presents the used system model and some basic notation. Three classical RMS-to-EDF schedulability quantifications are revisited in Section III. Section IV introduces the new measure Efficiency and derives formulas for the case of task sets consisting of two, three and n tasks. Next, the exact formulas of the assumed utilization distribution are derived in Section V. A summary with some discussion is provided in Section VI. Finally, a conclusion is drawn in Section VII.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL AND NOTATION
div.p: A periodic task (P i , e i ) with implicit deadlines (∀i : D i = P i ) is characterized by its period P i and its worstcase execution time (WCET) e i . A further parameter is the phase ϕ i . A synchronous (∀i : ϕ i = 0) task set consists of n such tasks. Since the synchronism establishes the worst case (critical instant) [1], other phasings are subsumed under this case. Preemptions are always allowed and happen in no time. There is no self-suspension of tasks.
The total utilization u is defined as sum of all individual task utilizations u i = e i /P i , thus u = n i=1 u i where n is the number of tasks in the task set.
We assume all task utilizations to be upper-bounded by u max . According to a necessary schedulability criterion, we need to choose u max = 1 in the most general case, ∀i :
The real-time tasks are executed on a uniprocessor system.

div.head: A. Breakdown Utilization (BU)
div.p: Task sets are randomly generated and then scaled (up or down) to the boundary separating RM-schedulable and RMunschedulable task sets [3]. The goal of Lehoczky et al. was the determination of a total utilization level where a breakdown of RMS schedulability typically occurs.

A severe problem here is that task sets with similar utilizations, a property complicating RM scheduling according to the Hyperbolic Bound (HB) (2) [19] formula and the difference of two squares formula (3), are higher weighted. From statistics, it is known that a (frequency) weight is the multiplicity a data point is contributing to a result. But, it is hard to give reasons for a greater importance of similarutilization task sets which could justify a translation of importance weights into frequency weights.
Note that in (3), ū = (u 1 + u 2 )/2 refers to the average utilization of two tasks and ∆u = u 2 -u 1 refers to the difference of the two utilizations 3 .
Thus, BU penalizes RMS more than EDF, cf. [9] for a discussion in more detail. BU is unfair since it weights EDFbeneficial cases higher.

div.head: B. Utilization Upper Bound (UUB)
div.p: The UUB describes the maximum possible utilization value for a sufficient schedulability test based on a simple total utilization comparison. All task sets up to a total utilization u ub are RM-schedulable. For task sets beyond this utilization level, there is no reliable statement on schedulability possible. Note that the index ub refers to "upper bound" here and in the following.

It is a common misconception to regard this utilization comparison as an exact, i.e., sufficient and necessary, test [8]. But, things are not such easy, and, RM schedulability is much more complex [8]. Beyond the UUB, only some task sets are RM-schedulable. However, UUB can give a first cue to RM schedulability since it correlates with the degree of period harmonicity of the task set.

Many authors have applied and refined this concept [1] [5] [6] [7]. In the most general domain, one obtains the famous Liu/Layland bound (1) [1] depending 4 only upon the number of tasks n. A problem with this measure is the complete ignorance of task sets in the "gray area" where the best utilization-based sufficient test fails, but the necessary criterion u ≤ 1 is fulfilled.

div.head: C. Numerical Optimality Degree (NOD)
div.p: The Optimality Degree (OD) of a scheduling algorithm A is defined as the ratio of the number of A-schedulable task sets to the number5 of task sets schedulable by an optimal algorithm [9]. In a more general approach, this optimal algorithm can be an arbitrary other algorithm. Then, a relative result is obtained.

The NOD is calculated by assuming a uniform distribution of total utilization u and integrating OD over u in the interval [0, 1], cf. [9]. This corresponds to averaging OD over all possible total utilizations. A problem here is the justification for a uniform total utilization distribution.

An argument that supports the choice of the uniform utilization distribution is Occam's razor. The lack of data on the concrete utilization distribution makes an assumption of the simplest possible one reasonable. On the other hand, other distributions can be assumed and are worth to be investigated. This is the motivation for our research. Later in Section V, it will turn out that the utilization follows a power-law distribution in our case.

A quantification of the RMS schedulability with respect to EDF exclusively based on the Liu/Layland and the Hyperbolic Bound was also investigated in [12]. There, a power-law utilization distribution was assumed, too. But there, nothing is said on this particular assumption and its justification. We think that our step-by-step explanations contribute to a better understanding. Besides a lower bound, we give additionally an upper bound which results in an enclosing of the exact performance gap value.

IV. A NEW EFFECTIVENESS MEASURE: EFFICIENCY Def.: Let A and B be two real-time scheduling algorithms. Then, A-to-B Efficiency is the conditional probability of a task set to be A-schedulable given that it is B-schedulable6 under the assumption of a power-law distribution of the total utilization, see Section V. This relative measure can be used as an absolute one by using an optimal scheduling algorithm B serving as the gold reference with an Efficiency of 100%.

We focus here on the uniprocessor case where EDF, a well-known optimal uniprocessor algorithm, is used as B and RMS, a very popular static-priority algorithm, is used as A. So, we are investigating the RMS-to-EDF Efficiency. In the following, when mentioning Efficiency, we mean this particular RMS-to-EDF Efficiency.

div.head: A. The Case of Two Tasks
div.p: Two basic concepts to be used in the following derivation of a formula are geometrical probability and the classical Laplace definition of probability, the ratio of favorable to possible cases.

We consider n = 2 tasks T 1 (P 1 , e 1 ) and T 2 (P 2 , e 2 ). When the period values are fixed, the tasks schedulable by EDF are obviously represented by the interior and the border of the triangle spanned by the vectors P 1 and P 2 in the e 1 e 2 plane, see Fig. 1.

The tasks schedulable by RMS are the interior and the border of a quadrangle which is the set difference of the EDF triangle and a triangle on the hypotenuse of the EDF triangle, see Fig. 1. Its top is the critical task set point C with the coordinates P 2 -P 1 and 2P 1 -P 2 in the e 1 e 2 plane in the special case P 1 ≤ P 2 < 2P 1 , cf. [1]. The possible cases (all task sets fulfilling the necessary RMS schedulability criterion u ≤ 1 which is the exact EDF schedulability criterion at the same time) are characterized by the triangle (0, 0)(P 1 , 0)(0, P 2 ). The favorable cases are represented by the hatched quadrangle in Fig. 1. This form of the area of favorable (RM-schedulable) cases is also justified by an application of the DCT7 schedulability test [20] which is sufficient in general, but for n = 2 an exact test as explained in [4].

The area ratio of these two regions is a reasonable measure of the effectiveness relation of RMS with respect to EDF since it follows the classical definition of probability, the favorable-to-possible-outcomes ratio, see (5). Note that the index pos means "possible" and f av means "favorable" in the following. The used approach is the application of the Laplacian definition of probability to dense parameter sets of infinite cardinality, yielding geometrical probabilities. Clearly, the number of tasks n in the task set serves in this context as the dimension of the geometrical objects. In the case of n = 2, this is areas, for n = 3 volumes, and for greater n values hypervolumes.

By a transformation from the execution time plane to the utilization plane, Fig. 2, (which is basically a normalization), the area ratio is clearly visible and formally derived in equations ( 6) and (7). Both equations use the triangle area formula base times corresponding height halved (4).

Note that ( 6) describes an isosceles right-angle triangle with two catheti of length one. Clearly, its area is 1/2 as it is the half of a unit square as shown in left-hand middle part of ( 6). The second way of obtaining this value is to take the triangle's hypotenuse as base which is shown in the right-hand middle part of (6). Both approaches lead to the consistent result of A pos = 1/2, cf. (6). Note further that u ub = 2 √ 2 -1 ≈ 0.828 is calculated as a special case of the Liu/Layland bound (1).

div.head: C. The Case of n Tasks
div.p: When regarding a task set of n tasks, the situation is yet more complicated. For this general case, we first suggest to use the Liu/Layland bound (1) [1] to obtain a lower Efficiency bound. It is more pessimistic than HB (2) [19], but in this context easier to operate with.

Note that the upper Efficiency bound is again u ub itself which equals the Liu/Layland bound (1). Then, the sufficient Liu/Layland criterion renders a hyperpyramid in the hyperspace of dimension n. This hyperpyramid is always similar to the one corresponding to the necessary criterion u ≤ 1. Thus, the volume ratio representing a lower LL-based Efficiency bound is given by the n-th power of (1), see (18). The reason is that isotropic scaling in n-dimensional space modifies the hypervolume of a hyperbody proportional to the n-th power of the (linear) scaling factor, see also Fig. 4.
div.formula: H fav, LL H pos = n( n √ 2 -1) n ≤ Eff RMS-to-EDF,n ≤ u ub (18)
div.p: Due to exponentiation, the LHS of ( 18) is quickly decreasing when n increases, no more giving a close bound. This behavior is also referred to as the curse of dimensionality, a term coined by Bellman in the context of mathematical optimization [22]. We have also found a general formula for the HBbased lower bound which is expected to yield a better approximation due to the advantages of the HB bound compared with the LL bound shown in [19]. First, the hypervolume of the region characterizing the possible cases meeting the necessary schedulability condition u ≤ 1 is needed. It is a n-sided hyperpyramid of dimension n with n edges of length 1. Note that for n = 1, it degenerates to a line segment of length 1. Another characterization of this polytope is a n-simplex 11 with an orthogonal corner at the origin of the coordinate system {u i |1 ≤ i ≤ n}. Its hypervolume is (20) as a generalization of (11). div.p: V. TOTAL UTILIZATION DISTRIBUTION As already discussed in Subsection III-C, the assumed distribution of the total utilization is crucial for estimating the drawback of RMS compared to EDF. At this stage, we clearly know that for calculating Efficiency, there is no longer a uniform distribution. Underlying utilization distributions weight higher utilizations more than lower utilizations. These qualitative statements shall be refined to quantitative ones in the following.

As common in mathematics, probability density function (pdf) and cumulative distribution function (cdf) are used to describe distributions. Note that these two functions are related to each other. The pdf is the derivative of the cdf. Conversely, the cdf is the definite integral of the pdf evaluated from -∞ to the argument value. The cdf is always a transition from zero to one. Equivalently, the definite integral of the pdf over the entire domain has to be 1.

div.head: A. The Case of Two Tasks
div.p: The frequency of task sets increases with the length of a u 2 = u -u 1 line in Fig. 2. Using the theorem on intersecting lines, the cardinal number of considered task sets grows linearly with the total utilization. Thus, the pdf is a linear function starting at the origin since only a single task set with utilization zero is taken into account 14 . The other constraint is that its integral over the interval [0, 1] is 1, see the introduction to Section V above. This gives already the pdf (26).
From it, the cdf is obtained by integration, yielding a quadratic function (27).

Note that the two formulas ( 26) and ( 27) implicitly assume a domain of total utilization u ∈ [0, 1], the only meaningful domain on a uniprocessor. As a result, we see that a quadratic utilization distribution is the underlying assumption in the case of n = 2 tasks. Note that this corresponds to the performance metric "weighted schedulability" presented in [18] where the weight also grows linearly with the total utilization.

div.head: B. The Case of Three Tasks
div.p: Here, the frequency of task sets grows with the area of triangles of equal total utilization, u 1 +u 2 +u 3 = u = const. According to a property of isotropic scaling, the area grows quadratically due to the two dimensions involved in area calculation. Again, only a single task set with total utilization zero is considered. Thus, the pdf needs to be of the form au 2 with the constant a. The constraint that the area under the pdf must equal one yields a = 3 and finally gives (28) for the pdf and by integration (29) for the cdf.
For three tasks, a cubic utilization distribution is assumed.

div.head: C. The Case of n Tasks
div.p: From the discussion for n = 2 and n = 3, we can generalize to the case of n tasks in a task set. The hyperplanes describing a constant utilization are then of dimensionality n -1. Hence, their hyperareas grow with a power of n -1 starting from zero for a zero total utilization. The general case of the utilization distribution is then described by its pdf (30) and its cdf (31).

Usually, power-law distributions are characterized by a negative exponent and a minimum15 value p(x) ∝ x -α with ∀x : x ≥ x min , see [25]. Here, we have the complementary case with total utilizations proportional to a power with a positive exponent and a maximum utilization u max = 1, cf. Section II.

This apparent discrepancy can be resolved by the substitution x := 1/u which is using the reciprocal total utilizations. Clearly, the inverse of the maximum utilization gives x min = 1/u max = 1. Matching the cdf P (x) = (x/x min ) -α+1 given in [25] with (31) using the substitution x := 1/u gives (32).
div.formula: F (u) = u u max α-1 = u α-1 = u n(32)
div.p: By equating coefficients, we see that n = α -1. But in [25], the complementary definition P (x) = Pr(X ≥ x) is used 16 . This is corrected by a simple vertical flip, giving P (x) = 1 -x -n which is then in conformance with the requirement that a cdf is always a transition from zero to one as given in the introduction of Section V.

Next, the pdf's can be reconciled, too. A straightforward approach is given by p(x)dx = (α -1)x α-1 min x -α dx as proposed in [25]. When replacing now x by 1/u, we obtain (33) which is in conformance with (30) when accepting the again necessary change of sign due to the uncommon definition of P (x) in [25].
div.formula: f (u)du = (α -1)u -α+1 max u α dx du du = (α -1)u -α+1 max u α -u -2 du = -(α -1)u -α+1 max u α-2 du = -(α -1)u α-2 du = -nu n-1 du(33)
div.p: Note that the chain rule is applied for performing the substitution correctly. The correcting factor to be inserted is the inner derivative dx du = -1 u 2 = -u -2 obtained using the elementary power rule of differentiation.

Summing up, for the general case of n tasks in the task set, their total utilizations follow a power-law probability distribution with exponent n. This means that high-utilization task sets are always higher weighted and their preference further increases when the number of tasks is increased. For n = 2 tasks in the task sets, the approach corresponds to the metric "weighted schedulability" proposed in [18]. For a more detailed explanation on the related concept of "weighted schedulability", see also the recently published PhD thesis [26], Section 6.2.2.

div.head: VI. SUMMARY A. Values and Graphs
div.p: In order to get an impression of the calculated bounds, we have computed the concrete values for n = 1..10. Note that 16 The usual definition of cdf is P (x) = Pr(X ≤ x). Although, due to equality, this is not a complement in the narrow sense, it can be considered as such since the probability of obtaining exactly a particular value is zero for continuous distributions. I. For the lower bounds, the maximum and thus, best, value is taken from the results of the different methods applied here. For clarification, we have added Fig. 5 showing these bounds including the improvement of the HBbased versus the LL-based approach.

A similar diagram is provided in [12] as Fig. 5 by Bini et al. But their diagram is the result of simulations working on synthetic task sets. Contrary to that, our diagram in Fig. 5 is based on an analytical evaluation which lead to formulas (18) and (25). Despite the fact that some of our results were obtained independently some years ago, we think that our framework of presentation with some new lines of argument can open a new view on scheduling algorithm performance metrics taking the kind of total utilization distribution into account.

Note that in [12], an additional corollary is that the advantage of the HB over the LL condition increases with the number of tasks n in the task set and tends to be a factor of √ 2 ≈ 1.414 for n → ∞.

div.head: B. Discussion
div.p: While the measure Efficiency is exactly known for n = 1, 2 tasks, there is a quickly increasing margin for task sets starting from n = 3 on. For larger n values, this margin becomes so large that only a qualitative statement is reasonable since the greatest known lower bound (25) converges to zero, lim n→∞ Hfav, HB Hpos = 0, and the least upper bound (1) converges to lim n→∞ n n √ 2 -1 = ln 2 ≈ 0.693. Clearly, Efficiency as a measure of schedulability of RM decreases with an increasing number of tasks. This behavior is in accordance with that of the three formerly presented metrics, Breakdown Utilization, Utilization Upper Bound and Numerical Optimality Degree, cf. Fig. 15 in [9].

But the new measure Efficiency turns out to be the most pessimistic one. While the basic approach of calculating ratios of counts of favorable and possible cases according to the classical Laplacian definition of probability is the same both for NOD and Efficiency, the assumptions on the distribution of the parameter total utilization u are different. NOD assumes u distributed uniformly in the interval [0, 1], cf. [9]. At first glance, this seems to be reasonable. But task sets with greater total utilizations are more difficult to schedule and should, thus, be higher weighted. This is reflected in the area/volume/hypervolume ratio approach when calculating Efficiency. Our method is a differential analysis. Low-utilization task sets are schedulable both by EDF and RMS and should not have the same impact as the more interesting high-utilization task sets.

As a spin-off, Fig. 5 clearly shows the superiority of the Hyperbolic Bound (2) to the Liu/Layland Bound (1) according to sensitivity or success ratio (in statistical terminology also called true positive rate, cf. [27]) of RM schedulability tests, defined as the cardinality of task sets deemed to be RM-schedulable to the cardinality of task sets actually being RM-schedulable. This is a confirmation of a result already shown in [19].

One possible objection to the new measure Efficiency is a too high weighting of task sets with a high total utilization, especially for task sets with a large number of tasks. This could apply for task sets starting from size n = 3 tasks on since for them, the weighting becomes supralinear. On the other hand, the consistent derivation of Efficiency from geometrical probability and Laplacian probability suggests the importance of the approach in spite of possible overweighting. Further, the higher weighting of high-utilization task sets in general is motivated by the fact that task sets being more difficult to schedule are attributed a higher value [18].

Second, it could be argued that Fig. 2 looks very similar to Fig. 2 in [9] where the breakdown utilization approach is criticized. This is true, but our area ratio approach ensures that all u 1 u 2 pairs in the triangle of possible task sets (with a total utilization not exceeding 1) are equally treated. On the isolines of utilization, there is no dominance of harder-to-schedule similar-utilization task sets. The weighting happens only by the parameter total utilization u. But the higher weighting of task sets with a greater total utilization is justified by a higher "value" of more-difficult-to-schedule task sets [18] in the context of a differential analysis. The total utilization distribution has been analyzed in Section V and is, thus, under control.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: A new measure of effectiveness of RMS compared to EDF coined Efficiency has been suggested and defined. By definition, it is a relative measure comparing two scheduling algorithms. Since EDF is an optimal uniprocessor scheduling algorithm, the RMS-to-EDF measure can also be regarded as an absolute one.

Up to now, exact values have been calculated only for task sets of n = 1 and n = 2 tasks. It turned out that for these two simple cases, Efficiency coincides with the well-known classical measure utilization upper bound, being u ub = 1 for n = 1 and u ub = 2( √ 2 -1) for n = 2. For greater n values, Efficiency is completely different from other classical measures. Exact values have not been calculated yet, but bounds have been given. Exact values are a challenge since an exact characterization of set differences between the EDF and the RM schedulability region in the general case would contradict the widely believed conjecture that RM schedulability is NP-Hard.

Compared to three other previously suggested schedulability measures, it is the most pessimistic one. A higher weighting of higher utilizations compared to NOD where a uniform total utilization distribution is assumed is the reason. This weighting is due to the intuition that highutilization task sets "[..] have higher 'value' since they are more difficult to schedule." [18] Like the other measures, RMS Efficiency decreases with an increasing number of tasks. The exact underlying total utilization distribution is a power-law distribution with exponent n.
Hence, we conclude that, for large task sets, RMS has a more significant deficiency in uniprocessor real-time schedulability compared to EDF than commonly believed.

As a byproduct, we have confirmed the superiority of the Hyperbolic Bound compared to the Liu/Layland Bound by evaluation of (hyper-)volume ratios. These hypervolumes are calculated as definite integrals.

In the future, we plan to tighten the bounds or even to calculate exact values of RMS-to-EDF Efficiency. If the closed-form evaluation of the RMS-to-EDF Efficiency turns out impossible, at least simulation results will be presented. Also, other algorithm choices for A and B shall be regarded when estimating A-to-B performance ratios. Since the RMSto-EDF performance ratio is by far the most important one on uniprocessor, a consideration of multiprocessor scheduling algorithms seems to be more relevant than further uniprocessor studies.
